questions.q: HIV is NOT spread by mosquito bites mainly because:
o: Mosquitoes never bite people infected with HIV
HIV is killed by the heat of the human body
The virus does not multiply in the mosquito, and the mosquito injects saliva, not earlier blood
Mosquito saliva contains antibodies against HIV
questions.x: HIV cannot replicate in insect cells, and when a mosquito feeds it injects only its saliva, not blood from a previous person. So the insect does not act as a vector.

questions.q: Doctors treat HIV with a combination of three or more different drugs instead of one drug. The main reason is that:
o: One drug alone kills too many helper T cells
Each drug works only on one organ
Combined drugs make the virus leave the body in urine
HIV mutates quickly, and several drugs together make drug-resistant virus far less likely
questions.x: Because HIV makes many copying errors, a single drug soon selects resistant mutants. A virus would need several mutations at once to escape a combination, so resistance develops much more slowly.

questions.q: In uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, cells cannot use glucose properly and respire much more fat. The person's respiratory quotient will:
questions.x: When fat becomes the main fuel, the RQ moves towards the fat value of about 0.7. An RQ of 1.0 reflects carbohydrate, and an RQ of zero would mean no carbon dioxide at all.

questions.q: A camel can go a long time without drinking partly because the fat stored in its hump, when oxidized, provides:
questions.x: Oxidation of fat releases a lot of energy and also produces water (metabolic water) from its many hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: One athlete runs a 100 m sprint and another runs a marathon. Which statement about their muscle respiration is correct?
o: Both rely only on anaerobic respiration
The sprinter relies more on anaerobic glycolysis; the marathon runner relies more on aerobic respiration, including fat oxidation
The marathon runner relies mainly on lactic acid fermentation
The sprinter relies mainly on beta-oxidation of fats
questions.x: A short sprint needs ATP faster than oxygen can be delivered, so anaerobic glycolysis supplies much of it. Long-distance running is mostly aerobic, and fat becomes an important fuel.

questions.q: One strand of DNA reads 5′-GATTC-3′. Written in the 5′ to 3′ direction, its complementary strand reads:
questions.x: The partner pairs base by base as 3′-CTAAG-5′. Because the strands are antiparallel, writing it from its 5′ end gives 5′-GAATC-3′.

questions.q: ATP is chemically close to an RNA nucleotide because it contains:
questions.x: ATP is adenosine (adenine + ribose) with three phosphate groups. Its sugar is ribose, the sugar of RNA, not deoxyribose.

questions.q: Sunflower seeds store mainly oil, while wheat grains store mainly starch. An advantage of oil as a store in a small, light seed is that oil:
o: Is soluble and moves easily through the seed
Can be used directly by the embryo without being broken down
Stores more energy in a smaller mass
questions.x: Gram for gram, oil yields about twice the energy of starch, so a light seed can carry a large energy reserve. Oil is insoluble, contains no nitrogen and must be broken down before use.

questions.q: Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein because its globin chains are combined with:
questions.x: Each globin chain carries a haem group, an iron-containing non-protein prosthetic group. This makes haemoglobin a conjugated (chromo)protein.

questions.q: How many molecules of water are used up when one diacylglycerol molecule is completely hydrolysed?
questions.x: A diacylglycerol has two ester bonds, one for each fatty acid. Hydrolysis of each ester bond uses one water molecule, so two are needed.

questions.q: In a typical phospholipid, the two fatty acids are attached to glycerol at:
o: All three carbons, with phosphate attached to a fatty acid
Carbon 2 only, with phosphate on carbons 1 and 3
Carbons 1 and 3, with no phosphate on glycerol
Carbons 1 and 2, with the phosphate group on carbon 3
questions.x: In a phospholipid, two hydroxyl groups of glycerol (carbons 1 and 2) are esterified with fatty acids, and the third (carbon 3) is linked to a phosphate group instead of a third fatty acid.

questions.q: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates because they:
o: Are always made of six carbon atoms
Cannot be hydrolysed into simpler sugars
questions.x: A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit and cannot be split into smaller sugars by hydrolysis. They range from three to seven carbons, are sweet and contain no nitrogen.

questions.q: The observation that in DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine and the amount of guanine equals cytosine was made by:
questions.x: Chargaff's base-ratio rules (A = T, G = C) were later explained by Watson and Crick's base pairing. Franklin produced X-ray pictures, Mendel studied inheritance in peas, and Griffith discovered transformation.

questions.q: In eukaryotic genes, the non-coding sequences that are removed from the RNA before translation are called:
questions.x: Introns are copied into the first RNA transcript and then cut out; the remaining exons are joined to form mature mRNA.

questions.q: In an amino acid, the amino group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R group are all attached to the:
questions.x: These four groups are all bonded to the central alpha (α) carbon. That is why the amino acids of proteins are called alpha amino acids.

questions.q: In water at about neutral pH, an amino acid exists mainly as a zwitterion, which carries:
o: Two positive charges and no negative charge
A positive –NH₃⁺ group and a negative –COO⁻ group on the same molecule
A negative –NH⁻ group and a positive –COOH₂⁺ group
questions.x: The carboxyl group loses H⁺ and the amino group gains H⁺, giving a dipolar ion with both charges. Its overall charge is zero.

questions.q: The narrow space between the inner and outer membranes of the nuclear envelope is called the:
questions.x: The two nuclear membranes are separated by the perinuclear space, which is continuous with the lumen of the ER. Nucleoplasm is the fluid inside the inner membrane.

questions.q: The main function of chromosomes is to:
o: Carry genes and pass hereditary information to daughter cells
questions.x: Chromosomes carry the genes made of DNA and hand an exact copy of them to each daughter cell at division.

questions.q: Stalked particles on the inner surface of the cristae, called F1 particles or oxysomes, are the sites of:
questions.x: The F1 particles are ATP synthase enzymes that make ATP using energy from electron transport. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Eukaryotic plasma membranes usually contain sterols such as cholesterol. Most bacterial membranes:
o: Contain more cholesterol than animal cells
questions.x: Sterols are a typical part of eukaryotic membranes; most bacteria lack them (mycoplasmas are an exception, taking sterols from their hosts).

questions.q: Lysosomes are common in animal cells. In most plant cells, much of the role of lysosomes is taken over by the:
questions.x: Lysosomes are rare in plant cells; their large vacuole contains hydrolytic enzymes and breaks down unwanted materials.

questions.q: In a withdrawal reflex with one interneuron, which pair of events BOTH take place inside the central nervous system?
o: Generation of the impulse in the receptor, and transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Contraction of the effector, and transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Transmission from sensory neuron to interneuron, and from interneuron to motor neuron
Generation of the impulse in the receptor, and transmission from sensory neuron to interneuron
questions.x: Both synapses involving the interneuron lie in the grey matter of the spinal cord. The receptor lies in the skin, and the neuromuscular junction and effector are in the limb, outside the CNS.

questions.q: When dust enters the eye, tears flow to wash it out. In this reflex the effector is the:
questions.x: Tears are secreted by the lacrimal gland, which is the effector here. The retina contains photoreceptors, and the iris muscle is the effector of the pupil reflex.

questions.q: The thalamus and hypothalamus together make up the part of the forebrain called the:
questions.x: The diencephalon is the part of the forebrain made of the thalamus and hypothalamus. The telencephalon forms the cerebrum, and the mesencephalon is the midbrain.

questions.q: Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus of the brain monitor the:
o: Oxygen content of the cerebrospinal fluid
Temperature of the blood flowing through it
Pressure of blood in the carotid arteries
questions.x: The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that sense blood temperature, which it uses to regulate body temperature. Blood pressure is sensed by baroreceptors in the arteries.

questions.q: Which feature of a neuron allows it to carry signals quickly over long distances, such as from the spinal cord to the foot?
o: A large nucleus in the cell body
A long axon covered with a myelin sheath
Many Nissl's granules in the cell body
questions.x: A long axon reaches distant effectors and its myelin sheath speeds conduction. Dendrites receive signals and Nissl's granules make proteins.

questions.q: The sodium–potassium pump helps keep the inside of a resting neuron negative because it:
o: Brings negative chloride ions into the cell
Moves more positive charges out than it brings in
Moves equal numbers of ions in each direction
Pumps protein anions out of the cell
questions.x: By moving three Na+ out for every two K+ in, the pump removes more positive charge than it adds. Protein anions stay inside the cell.

questions.q: In a myelinated peripheral nerve fibre, the correct order of layers from the centre outwards is:
questions.x: The Schwann cell wraps its membrane many times around the axon to form myelin; its outer layer with nucleus and cytoplasm is the neurilemma.

questions.q: The vasomotor centre, which controls the diameter of blood vessels and so helps regulate blood pressure, lies in the:
questions.x: The medulla contains vital centres for heartbeat, breathing and blood vessel diameter (vasomotor centre). The cerebellum coordinates movement and the occipital lobe deals with vision.

questions.q: Salivary amylase acting on starch produces mainly:
questions.x: Amylase breaks starch into the disaccharide maltose; maltase later splits maltose into glucose. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose.

questions.q: Protein-digesting enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin are secreted in an inactive form mainly to:
o: Make them work faster at low pH
Let them pass through membranes as lipids
Protect the cells that make them from being digested
questions.x: If they were active inside the cells that make them, these proteases would digest the cells' own proteins. They are activated only in the gut.

questions.q: During non-competitive inhibition, can the substrate and the inhibitor occupy one enzyme molecule simultaneously?
o: No, because they compete for the active site
No, because the inhibitor destroys the enzyme first
Yes, because they bind at different sites
Yes, because the inhibitor is identical to the substrate
questions.x: A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme, so the substrate can still occupy the active site, but it is converted poorly or not at all.

questions.q: The antibiotic penicillin kills bacteria by:
o: Inhibiting an enzyme that bacteria need to build their cell walls
Denaturing all bacterial proteins by heat
Acting as a coenzyme for bacteria
questions.x: Penicillin blocks a bacterial enzyme that makes cross-links in the cell wall. Without a strong wall the bacteria burst.

questions.q: Pasteur's swan-necked flask experiment showed that:
o: Microorganisms arise spontaneously from boiled broth
Air contains a vital force needed to make life
Organic molecules can form from inorganic gases
Microorganisms arise only from pre-existing microorganisms
questions.x: Boiled broth in a swan-necked flask stayed free of microbes because dust and microbes were trapped in the bent neck. This supported biogenesis and disproved spontaneous generation under present conditions.

questions.q: Stanley Miller carried out his famous experiment on the origin of organic molecules while working as a student of:
questions.x: Miller was a graduate student of Harold Urey at the University of Chicago, which is why it is called the Miller–Urey experiment. Oparin and Haldane proposed the hypothesis that the experiment tested.

questions.q: Darwin chose the term 'natural selection' because he saw that:
o: Nature creates new organs when they are needed
Nature, like a breeder, decides which individuals survive and breed
Every individual in nature breeds equally
Nature selects which acquired characters are inherited
questions.x: Darwin compared nature with a breeder choosing animals to breed. In nature, the environment 'chooses' by letting better-suited individuals leave more offspring.

questions.q: The scientist who cut the tails of mice to test inheritance of acquired characters, August Weismann, was a:
questions.x: August Weismann was a German biologist. He is known for the germplasm theory and for his experiments on mice.

questions.q: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) in early pregnancy is secreted by the:
o: Developing embryo (its chorion, which forms part of the placenta)
questions.x: hCG is made by the chorion of the early embryo. It keeps the corpus luteum alive so that progesterone stays high.

questions.q: The causative agent of AIDS is:
questions.x: AIDS is caused by HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus. Herpes simplex causes genital herpes, Treponema causes syphilis and Neisseria causes gonorrhoea.

questions.q: HIV is NOT spread by:
o: Unprotected sex with an infected person
Sharing razors used by an infected person
questions.x: Mosquitoes do not transmit HIV; the virus does not multiply in them. Sex, shared razors and breast milk can all carry infected body fluids.

questions.q: The crescent-shaped menisci that cushion the knee joint between the femur and the tibia are made of:
questions.x: The menisci are fibrocartilage, whose thick collagen bundles resist pressure and absorb shock. Hyaline cartilage covers the bone ends but does not form the menisci.

questions.q: A skeletal muscle fibre has many nuclei because, in the embryo, it is formed by:
o: Taking up nuclei from the nerves that supply it
Splitting of one large cell into many smaller ones
questions.x: Each skeletal muscle fibre develops when many embryonic muscle-forming cells fuse end to end, so the fibre keeps all their nuclei. Nerves do not pass nuclei to muscle.

questions.q: In compact bone, the Haversian canals run:
o: At right angles to the long axis of the bone
Only through the spongy ends of the bone
Only beneath the cartilage at joint surfaces
Parallel to the long axis of the bone
questions.x: Haversian (central) canals run lengthwise, parallel to the long axis. The canals running across the bone at right angles are Volkmann's canals.

questions.q: The cartilages of the larynx help mainly by:
o: Keeping the airway open and supporting the vocal cords
Producing blood cells for the throat
questions.x: The firm but flexible laryngeal cartilages hold the airway open and support the vocal cords for voice production. Cartilage has no marrow, so it cannot make blood cells.

questions.q: The number of phalanges in each human hand is:
questions.x: The thumb has two phalanges and each of the other four fingers has three, giving 2 + 12 = 14.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of events in one cross-bridge cycle?
o: Head attaches to actin → power stroke → ATP binds and head detaches → ATP split, head re-cocked
ATP binds → head attaches to actin → ATP split → power stroke
Power stroke → head attaches to actin → ATP split → ATP binds
Head detaches → power stroke → head attaches → ATP binds
questions.x: The energised head binds actin, swings in the power stroke, then a new ATP binds and releases it; splitting that ATP re-cocks the head for the next cycle. The power stroke cannot happen before the head is attached.

questions.q: How are myofibrils oriented inside a long striated muscle cell?
o: At right angles to the long axis of the fibre
In a random network through the sarcoplasm
Parallel to the long axis of the fibre
In a spiral around the nuclei
questions.x: Myofibrils lie side by side along the length of the fibre. Because they run parallel to the long axis, their shortening shortens the whole fibre.

questions.q: The term 'excitation–contraction coupling' refers to:
o: The joining of two muscles in an antagonistic pair
The link by which an action potential on the sarcolemma causes calcium release inside the fibre
The binding of ATP to the myosin head
The fusion of myoblasts to form a muscle fibre
questions.x: Excitation (the action potential) is coupled to contraction when the impulse travels down the T-tubules and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The other options are separate processes.

questions.q: In four o'clock plants, flower colour shows incomplete dominance. A pink-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant. The offspring are expected to be:
questions.x: Pink is RW and white is WW. RW × WW gives 1 RW (pink) : 1 WW (white). The 1 : 2 : 1 ratio comes only from pink × pink.

questions.q: In a dihybrid F2 (AaBb × AaBb), what fraction of the offspring shows the dominant phenotype for gene A, whatever its phenotype for gene B?
questions.x: Because gene B assorts independently, it does not affect the result for gene A: Aa × Aa gives 3/4 A_. 9/16 is the fraction dominant for both genes.

questions.q: In the F2 of a monohybrid cross (Tt × Tt), the ratio of homozygous plants to heterozygous plants is:
questions.x: The F2 is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Homozygous plants (TT + tt) are 2 out of 4 and heterozygous (Tt) are 2 out of 4, giving 1 : 1.

questions.q: Compared with two genes that assort independently, two tightly linked genes:
o: Increase the number of recombinant offspring
Reduce the variety of allele combinations among the offspring
Give the four test-cross classes in equal numbers
Are separated in every meiotic division
questions.x: Tightly linked genes rarely separate, so most offspring repeat the parental combinations and fewer new combinations appear.

questions.q: If Xʷ is the white-eye allele, a white-eyed male Drosophila has the genotype:
questions.x: The white-eye gene is on the X chromosome and absent from the Y, so a white-eyed male carries one Xʷ with a Y.

questions.q: Two individuals heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb) are crossed. The chance that an offspring is heterozygous for the first gene but homozygous recessive for the second is:
questions.x: P(Aa) from Aa × Aa is 1/2 and P(bb) from Bb × Bb is 1/4. Since the genes assort independently, 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

questions.q: Mendel crossed pure-breeding RRYY peas with pure-breeding rryy peas. What is true of the genotype of each F1 hybrid?
o: It carries two dominant alleles of each gene (RRYY)
It carries two recessive alleles of each gene (rryy)
It is heterozygous for seed shape only (RrYY)
It carries one dominant and one recessive allele of each gene (RrYy)
questions.x: The RRYY parent gives only RY gametes and the rryy parent only ry gametes, so every F1 plant is RrYy, with round yellow seeds.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares autosomes and sex chromosomes in humans?
o: Autosomes are alike in both sexes, while the sex chromosome pair differs
Autosomes differ between males and females
Sex chromosomes carry only genes for sex
Autosomes are found only in body cells, not in gametes
questions.x: The 22 pairs of autosomes are the same in males and females; only the sex chromosome pair differs (XX or XY). The X also carries many genes not linked to sex, and gametes contain autosomes too.

questions.q: The carotid arteries supply blood to the:
questions.x: The carotid arteries run up the neck to the head and brain. The arms are supplied by the subclavian arteries and the kidneys by the renal arteries.

questions.q: The short interval between the 'lubb' and the 'dubb' sounds corresponds to:
questions.x: 'Lubb' marks the start of ventricular systole and 'dubb' marks its end, so the time between them is the period when the ventricles are contracting.

questions.q: Blood capillaries connect:
questions.x: Blood flows from arterioles into capillaries and then into venules. Capillaries do not open into the heart or the lymph ducts.

questions.q: Arteriosclerosis refers to:
o: Swelling of veins caused by weak valves
Hardening of the artery walls, with loss of their elasticity
questions.x: In arteriosclerosis the artery walls become thick and stiff, often by calcium deposits, so they can no longer stretch and recoil with each beat.

questions.q: Which organ is NOT part of the lymphatic system?
questions.x: The spleen, thymus and tonsils are lymphoid organs. The pancreas is a digestive and endocrine gland.

questions.q: An allergy is best described as:
o: A failure to make any antibodies
An immune attack on the body's own cells
An excessive immune response to a normally harmless substance
Immunity passed from mother to baby
questions.x: In an allergy the immune system overreacts to harmless substances such as pollen or dust. Attacking one's own cells is autoimmunity.

questions.q: Arrange the steps by which T cells clear a virus infection in their proper sequence:
o: Cytotoxic T cells multiply → antigen displayed by a macrophage → helper T cell activated → infected cells killed
Helper T cell activated → infected cells killed → antigen displayed by a macrophage → cytotoxic T cells multiply
Antigen displayed by a macrophage → helper T cell activated → cytotoxic T cells multiply → infected cells killed
Infected cells killed → cytotoxic T cells multiply → helper T cell activated → antigen displayed by a macrophage
questions.x: A macrophage first presents the antigen, which activates helper T cells. Their cytokines make matching cytotoxic T cells divide into a clone, and these kill the infected cells.

questions.q: How many lobes does the right lung of a human have?
questions.x: The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle and lower). The left lung has only two lobes because part of the space on the left is taken up by the heart.

questions.q: Which change happens within about a day of a smoker stopping smoking?
o: Destroyed alveolar walls are fully rebuilt
The carbon monoxide level in the blood falls towards normal
questions.x: Carbon monoxide is gradually breathed out once no more is inhaled, so the carboxyhaemoglobin level drops to near normal within about a day. Alveolar damage from emphysema is permanent, and cancer does not simply go away.

questions.q: If a person's diaphragm were paralysed but the external intercostal muscles still worked normally, the person would:
o: Still be able to breathe in, but less deeply than normal
Be completely unable to breathe in
Breathe in more deeply than normal
Be able to breathe in only by contracting the internal intercostals
questions.x: Inspiration is produced by both the diaphragm and the external intercostals. With the diaphragm out of action, raising the ribs alone can still enlarge the thorax, but by less, so breaths are shallower. Internal intercostals help forced expiration, not inspiration.

questions.q: The stomach lies in the:
o: Lower right part of the abdomen, near the appendix
Upper left part of the abdomen, just below the diaphragm
Pelvic cavity, above the urinary bladder
questions.x: The J-shaped stomach lies in the upper left abdomen, immediately below the diaphragm, with the liver mostly to its right.

questions.q: Which statement about the position of the liver is correct?
o: It lies in the lower left abdomen
It lies in the thorax, between the lungs
It lies in the upper right abdomen, just below the diaphragm
It lies in the pelvic cavity, behind the bladder
questions.x: The liver, the largest gland, occupies the upper right part of the abdomen just under the diaphragm, partly covering the stomach.

questions.q: Lactase in the small intestine digests milk sugar (lactose) into:
questions.x: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose, so lactase releases these two. Sucrase gives glucose and fructose, and maltase gives two glucose molecules.

questions.q: The kidneys receive a very large blood flow for their small size. The main reason is that:
o: The kidneys store blood for emergencies
The kidneys make red blood cells
A large volume of plasma must pass through the glomeruli to be filtered
The kidneys need it to keep the body warm
questions.x: The kidneys receive roughly a fifth to a quarter of the blood pumped by the heart. Such a flow lets them filter the whole plasma many times a day, far more than their own oxygen needs.

questions.q: Blood enters each kidney through the:
questions.x: The renal artery brings blood in; it branches to supply the afferent arterioles of the glomeruli. The renal vein takes blood out, and the ureter carries urine.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts glomerular filtration with selective reabsorption?
o: Filtration is active and selective; reabsorption is entirely passive
Filtration is passive and depends on molecule size; much reabsorption is active and selective
Both are passive processes driven by blood pressure
Filtration takes place in the PCT, and reabsorption in Bowman's capsule
questions.x: Filtration is driven by blood pressure and lets through everything small enough, useful or not. Reabsorption picks out useful substances, often by active transport using ATP.

questions.q: Which of the following is a normal component of healthy human urine?
questions.x: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste in urine. Glucose is normally all reabsorbed, and albumin and red cells are not filtered, so their presence suggests disease.

questions.q: Which statement about uric acid is correct?
o: It is only slightly soluble, so it can be passed out with very little water
It is a gas excreted through the lungs
It is more toxic than ammonia
It is the main waste of bony fishes
questions.x: Uric acid's low solubility lets it be excreted as crystals or paste, saving water. It is the least toxic of the three main wastes.

questions.q: In peritoneal dialysis the fluid contains a high concentration of glucose. This helps to:
o: Feed the cells of the peritoneum
Draw excess water out of the blood by osmosis
questions.x: The glucose makes the fluid hypertonic to the blood, so water moves out of the blood across the peritoneum by osmosis, removing the extra water that the kidneys cannot.

questions.q: Which nitrogenous waste is produced at a fairly steady daily rate that depends mainly on a person's muscle mass?
questions.x: Creatinine comes from creatine phosphate in muscle, so its output is steady. Urea output varies with protein intake.

questions.q: Compared with plasma, what is the tonicity of the filtrate in Bowman's capsule, then at the tip of a long loop of Henle, then at the start of the DCT?
questions.x: Filtrate starts isotonic. It loses water in the descending limb, so it is hypertonic at the hairpin, then loses salt without water in the ascending limb, so it enters the DCT hypotonic.

questions.q: A rise in the osmotic concentration of the blood causes more ADH release and also:
o: A feeling of thirst, which leads to drinking
questions.x: The hypothalamus, which senses blood concentration, also contains the thirst centre. Drinking adds water while ADH saves it, and both bring the concentration back to normal.

questions.q: Which of the following medicines made by biotechnology is an enzyme?
questions.x: tPA is a protease enzyme that converts plasminogen into plasmin. Insulin, growth hormone and erythropoietin are hormones, not enzymes.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat some cancers because they:
o: Copy the DNA of cancer cells
Bind specifically to antigens on cancer cells and can carry drugs to them or mark them for destruction
Replace the faulty gene in every body cell
Increase the division rate of all cells
questions.x: A monoclonal antibody recognises one antigen on the cancer cell, so it can deliver an attached drug or toxin straight to it or flag it for the immune system, sparing most normal cells.

questions.q: For producing vaccines, influenza and some other viruses are grown in large numbers in:
o: Fertilised hen's eggs or cultures of living cells
questions.x: Viruses multiply only inside living cells, so they are grown in embryonated (fertilised) eggs or in animal cell cultures. Nutrient agar supports bacteria and fungi, not viruses.

questions.q: To find the limiting reactant from the amounts of two reactants, a student should compare:
o: The masses of the two reactants taken
The molar masses of the two reactants
The moles of each reactant divided by its coefficient in the balanced equation
The volumes of the two reactants, whatever their states
questions.x: Dividing each reactant's moles by its coefficient shows how many 'reaction units' it can supply; the smallest value is the limiting reactant. Comparing masses ignores both molar mass and the mole ratio.

questions.q: Carbon burns as C + O₂ → CO₂ with a percentage yield of 50%. What mass of carbon must be burnt to collect 22 g of CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.x: At 50% yield the theoretical CO₂ must be 44 g = 1 mol, which needs 1 mol = 12 g of carbon. 6 g gives only 11 g of CO₂ at this yield.

questions.q: Phosphorus (Z = 15) has how many half-filled 3p orbitals in its ground state?
questions.x: P is [Ne] 3s² 3p³. By Hund's rule the three 3p electrons occupy the three 3p orbitals singly, so all three are half-filled.

questions.q: Which pair of orbitals belongs to the same subshell?
questions.x: 3px and 3pz have the same n (3) and l (1), so both are in the 3p subshell. The other pairs differ in n or in l.

questions.q: Which subshell contains the largest number of orbitals?
questions.x: The number of orbitals depends on l, not n: f has 7, d has 5, p has 3 and s has 1.

questions.q: More gas is pumped into a rigid container at constant temperature, and the pressure rises. According to the kinetic molecular theory, this is because:
o: Each collision with the wall is now more forceful
The molecules now attract one another more strongly
More molecules strike the walls every second
questions.x: At constant temperature the average speed, and so the force of each impact, is unchanged. More molecules in the same space means more impacts per second, so the pressure rises.

questions.q: The motion in which gas molecules move as a whole from one place to another is called:
questions.x: Translational motion carries a molecule from one place to another, and it is the motion responsible for gas pressure and diffusion. Vibration and rotation do not move the molecule through space.

questions.q: A gas exerts the same pressure on every wall of its container. According to the kinetic molecular theory, this is because:
o: Molecular motion is random, so on average every part of the wall is struck equally often
Molecules move faster towards the top of the container
Molecules attract each wall with the same force
The heavier molecules always settle at the bottom
questions.x: Random motion means no direction is preferred, so each area of wall receives the same number of impacts per second on average. Gravity has a negligible effect on a gas in a small container.

questions.q: Boyle's law holds only when:
o: The mass and the temperature of the gas are kept constant
The pressure and the temperature of the gas are kept constant
The volume and the mass of the gas are kept constant
The pressure and the volume of the gas are kept constant
questions.x: Boyle's law relates pressure and volume, so both of these change, while the amount (mass) of gas and its temperature are fixed.

questions.q: How many lone pairs on the nitrogen atom of an NH₃ molecule are available to accept hydrogen bonds?
questions.x: N has five valence electrons: three are used in N–H bonds, leaving one lone pair. Oxygen in water has two.

questions.q: Isomorphism is the existence of:
o: One substance in two or more crystal forms
A substance with no definite crystal shape
A crystal with different properties in different directions
Different substances in the same crystal form
questions.x: Isomorphous substances are different compounds with the same crystal structure. One substance in several crystal forms is polymorphism.

questions.q: An imaginary plane divides a crystal into two parts that are exact mirror images of each other. This plane is called a:
questions.x: A plane that gives two mirror-image halves is a plane of symmetry. A cleavage plane is a direction along which the crystal splits, not a symmetry element.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the reverse reaction is:
o: The combination of H₂ and I₂ to form HI
The decomposition of HI into H₂ and I₂
The burning of hydrogen in iodine vapour
The ionisation of HI in water
questions.x: The reverse reaction runs right to left: 2HI → H₂ + I₂. Combination of H₂ and I₂ is the forward reaction.

questions.q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), the volume of the vessel is increased at constant temperature, lowering the pressure. The equilibrium:
o: Shifts to the left, towards fewer gas molecules
Shifts to the right, towards more gas molecules
Does not shift, as Kc is unchanged
Shifts to the left and Kc decreases
questions.x: Lower pressure favours the side with more moles of gas: 2 on the right against 1 on the left, so more PCl₅ dissociates.

questions.q: Ksp of Mg(OH)₂ is 1 × 10⁻¹¹. If [OH⁻] is fixed at 0.1 mol dm⁻³ by dissolved NaOH, the concentration of Mg²⁺ that can remain in solution is:
questions.x: Ksp = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]², so [Mg²⁺] = 1 × 10⁻¹¹/(0.1)² = 1 × 10⁻⁹. Forgetting to square [OH⁻] gives 1 × 10⁻¹⁰.

questions.q: Which statement about the molecularity of an elementary step is correct?
o: It can be zero or fractional, like the order
It is always a whole number and can never be zero
It can be found only by experiment from the rate equation
It applies only to the overall equation, not to single steps
questions.x: Molecularity is the number of particles taking part in one elementary step, so it is 1, 2 or (rarely) 3. Zero or fractional values are possible for order, not molecularity.

questions.q: If a reaction had an activation energy of zero, then:
o: Every collision with the proper orientation would lead to reaction
The reaction would not take place at all
The reaction would have to be endothermic
Its rate would not depend on how often the particles collide
questions.x: With no energy barrier, energy is no longer a requirement; only correct orientation limits the reaction, and the rate depends on collision frequency.

questions.q: A change in which no heat enters or leaves the system, because the system is thermally insulated, is called:
questions.x: Adiabatic means q = 0. Isothermal is constant temperature, isobaric constant pressure and isochoric constant volume.

questions.q: Bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
questions.x: Bonds broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ; bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: In the older CGS system, energy is measured in ergs. One joule is equal to:
questions.x: 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻² = 1000 g × 10⁴ cm² s⁻² = 10⁷ g cm² s⁻² = 10⁷ erg.

questions.q: In the reaction 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, which statement is correct?
o: Fe²⁺ is reduced and Cl₂ is the reducing agent
Fe²⁺ is oxidised and Cl₂ is the oxidising agent
questions.x: Iron rises from +2 to +3 (oxidised), while chlorine falls from 0 to −1, so Cl₂ is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

questions.q: During electrolysis, positive ions (cations) in the electrolyte move towards the:
questions.x: In electrolysis the cathode is negative, so cations are attracted to it and gain electrons there.

questions.q: Which liquid mixes completely with water?
questions.x: Propanone is polar (C=O group) and forms hydrogen bonds with water through its oxygen, so it mixes in all proportions. The other three are non-polar.

questions.q: A covalent bond between two different atoms has some ionic character because:
o: The shared electron pair is pulled more towards the more electronegative atom
Electrons are completely transferred from one atom to the other
Both atoms have exactly the same electronegativity
The bond contains a lone pair
questions.x: When the atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared pair lies closer to one atom, which gets a partial negative charge. Complete transfer would make the bond fully ionic.

questions.q: When one s orbital mixes with three p orbitals, the number of hybrid orbitals formed is:
questions.x: The number of hybrid orbitals always equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed: 1 s + 3 p gives four sp³ hybrid orbitals.

questions.q: The anion present in sodium peroxide is:
questions.x: Peroxides contain the O₂²⁻ ion with oxygen at −1. O²⁻ is the oxide ion and O₂⁻ is the superoxide ion.

questions.q: Moving across the first transition series, the first ground-state atom to have a completely filled 3d subshell is:
questions.x: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, so the 3d subshell becomes full one element before zinc (3d¹⁰ 4s²). Nickel is still 3d⁸ and cobalt 3d⁷.

questions.q: Cis and trans isomers of an alkene do not change into each other at room temperature because:
o: The two isomers have different molecular formulas
The C=C bond rotates freely and quickly
The isomers are always mirror images of each other
Rotation about the C=C bond would require breaking the π bond
questions.x: The π bond holds the two carbons in a fixed position; turning one end would break it, which needs much more energy than is available at room temperature.

questions.q: The two types of stereoisomerism are:
questions.x: Stereoisomers differ only in the arrangement of atoms in space: geometric and optical. Chain, position and functional group isomerism are structural.

questions.q: How does the number of π bonds in the organic reactant change in addition and in substitution reactions?
o: It increases in addition but decreases in substitution
It stays the same in addition but decreases in substitution
It decreases in addition but stays the same in substitution
It decreases in both types of reaction
questions.x: Addition uses π bonds to form new σ bonds, so unsaturation falls. In substitution one atom or group simply replaces another, so the number of π bonds does not change.

questions.q: The AlCl₃ used in Friedel–Crafts reactions must be anhydrous because:
o: Water reacts with AlCl₃ so that it can no longer act as a Lewis acid catalyst
Water reacts with benzene to form phenol
Anhydrous AlCl₃ is the electrophile that enters the ring
Water would make the reaction explosive
questions.x: AlCl₃ is hydrolysed by water, losing its ability to accept a pair of electrons. It then cannot generate the carbocation or acylium ion.

questions.q: Which statement about the structure of benzene is NOT correct?
o: Each carbon atom is sp² hybridised
All twelve atoms lie in one plane
Each bond angle in the ring is 120°
It contains three short C=C bonds and three long C–C bonds
questions.x: All six C–C bonds in benzene have the same length, 1.39 Å, because the π electrons are delocalised. The other statements are correct.

questions.q: Which IUPAC name fits the alkyne CH₃–C≡C–C(CH₃)₃, which carries a tert-butyl group?
questions.x: The longest chain through the triple bond has five carbons. Numbering from the CH₃ end next to the triple bond gives the triple bond position 2 and both methyls position 4.

questions.q: Cyclohexene and benzene are each hydrogenated over a nickel catalyst. Which statement is correct?
o: Cyclohexene needs more severe conditions than benzene
Benzene needs more severe conditions (higher temperature and pressure) than cyclohexene
Both react with hydrogen at room temperature without a catalyst
questions.x: The localised C=C bond of cyclohexene is hydrogenated easily. Benzene's resonance-stabilised ring resists addition, so higher temperature and pressure are needed.

questions.q: Which of the following species is NOT an electrophile?
questions.x: NH₃ has a lone pair to donate, so it is a nucleophile. NO₂⁺, Cl⁺ and SO₃ are electron-seeking species that attack the benzene ring.

questions.q: At the end of the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃, the FeBr₃:
o: Is used up and turned into iron metal
Is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst
questions.x: FeBr₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the arenium ion, giving HBr and FeBr₃ again. Since it is not used up, FeBr₃ is a catalyst.

questions.q: Applying IUPAC rules, including alphabetical order when locants tie, CH₃CHBrCH(CH₃)CH₃ is named:
questions.x: The longest chain has four carbons, and either direction gives the locants 2 and 3. When locants tie, the substituent first in alphabetical order (bromo) gets the lower number.

questions.q: Ethanol reacts with phosphorus trichloride: 3C₂H₅OH + PCl₃ → 3C₂H₅Cl + ?. The other product is:
questions.x: With PCl₃ the by-product is phosphorous acid, H₃PO₃. POCl₃ and HCl are the by-products when PCl₅ is used instead.

questions.q: The rate of reaction of alcohols with metallic sodium, in which the O–H bond breaks, follows the order:
o: All three react at the same rate
questions.x: Alkyl groups push electrons towards oxygen, making the O–H hydrogen harder to remove. A tertiary alcohol has the most alkyl groups, so it reacts most slowly with sodium; this is the reverse of the Lucas test order.

questions.q: Which statement about the nitration of phenol and of benzene is correct?
o: Both need a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ at 55 °C
Benzene is nitrated by dilute HNO₃; phenol needs concentrated acids
Phenol is nitrated by dilute HNO₃ at room temperature; benzene needs concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄
Neither can be nitrated without a FeCl₃ catalyst
questions.x: The activated ring of phenol reacts even with dilute nitric acid in the cold. Benzene needs the nitrating mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids to produce enough NO₂⁺.

questions.q: The smallest possible ketone contains how many carbon atoms?
questions.x: In a ketone the carbonyl carbon must be bonded to two other carbon atoms, so the smallest is propanone, CH₃COCH₃, with three carbons. One- and two-carbon carbonyl compounds are aldehydes.

questions.q: Acetaldehyde is the common name of:
questions.x: Acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO, is ethanal. Methanal is formaldehyde and propanone is acetone.

questions.q: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is a stronger acid than 4-chlorobutanoic acid. The reason is that:
o: Chlorine releases electrons when it is close to the –COOH group
The inductive effect of chlorine weakens with distance, so it stabilises the anion more when closer to –COOH
2-chlorobutanoic acid forms hydrogen bonds but 4-chlorobutanoic acid cannot
questions.x: Both have the same formula; the −I effect falls off quickly along the chain, so chlorine on C-2 withdraws electrons from the carboxylate far more than on C-4.

questions.q: Which of the following is a fibrous protein?
questions.x: Keratin of hair and nails has long, parallel chains and is insoluble in water, which is typical of fibrous proteins. Insulin, haemoglobin and albumin are compact, soluble globular proteins.

questions.q: A rubber-based contact adhesive is spread on both surfaces and left for a few minutes before they are pressed together. The waiting time allows:
o: The resin and hardener to react
Moisture from the air to start polymerisation
The molten adhesive to cool and solidify
The solvent to evaporate so the films become tacky
questions.x: Contact adhesives are dissolved in a volatile solvent; once most of it evaporates, the tacky films bond instantly on contact. Resin and hardener describe epoxy adhesives.

questions.q: Adding the vectors 3î + 4ĵ and î − 4ĵ gives a resultant of:
questions.x: Adding components: x = 3 + 1 = 4 and y = 4 − 4 = 0. The resultant is 4î, i.e. 4 units along the positive x-axis.

questions.q: Two identical balls collide head-on and perfectly elastically. Before the collision one moves at 4 m s⁻¹ forward and the other at 2 m s⁻¹ backward. After the collision:
o: The first moves at 2 m s⁻¹ backward and the second at 4 m s⁻¹ forward
Both move forward at 1 m s⁻¹
The first moves at 4 m s⁻¹ backward and the second at 2 m s⁻¹ forward
questions.x: In a head-on elastic collision between equal masses the bodies simply exchange velocities. Check: momentum 4 − 2 = 2 before and −2 + 4 = 2 after.

questions.q: A body of mass m moving at speed v hits an identical body at rest, and the two stick together. The fraction of the original kinetic energy lost is:
questions.x: Common velocity = v/2. KE after = ½(2m)(v/2)² = ¼mv², which is half of the original ½mv². So half the kinetic energy is lost.

questions.q: A ball is launched at 20√2 m s⁻¹ at 45° above the horizontal (cos 45° = 1/√2). Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity 2 s after launch is:
questions.x: Horizontal component = 20√2 × (1/√2) = 20 m s⁻¹, and it does not change during the flight, so it is still 20 m s⁻¹ after 2 s.

questions.q: A particle moves along a circle of radius 5 m and turns through an angle of 60° about the centre. The magnitude of its displacement is (sin 30° = 0.5):
questions.x: The displacement is the chord: 2r sin(60°/2) = 2 × 5 × 0.5 = 5 m. The two radii and the chord form an equilateral triangle. 5π/3 m is the arc length (distance).

questions.q: Which of the following collisions is perfectly elastic?
o: A lump of clay hitting a wall and sticking
A bullet embedding itself in a wooden block
A car crash in which the cars crumple
Collisions between molecules of an ideal gas
questions.x: Kinetic theory treats collisions between ideal gas molecules as perfectly elastic. In the other cases the bodies deform or stick, so kinetic energy is lost.

questions.q: A dart is thrown horizontally, aimed exactly at the centre of a dartboard. It hits the board a little below the centre because:
o: Its horizontal velocity decreases during the flight
It falls vertically under gravity while it moves horizontally
Gravity acts on it only after it slows down
Its horizontal and vertical velocities cancel
questions.x: During its time of flight the dart accelerates downward at g while moving horizontally, so it drops below the line along which it was aimed.

questions.q: How much work must be done on a 3 kg trolley on a smooth level floor to increase its speed from 2 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹?
questions.x: Work = change in KE = ½ × 3 × (4² − 2²) = 1.5 × 12 = 18 J. Squaring the change in speed, ½ × 3 × 2², gives the wrong 6 J.

questions.q: A 3 kg lamp hangs 3 m below a ceiling. If the ceiling is taken as the reference level, the gravitational potential energy of the lamp is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: The lamp is 3 m below the reference level, so h = −3 m and PE = 3 × 10 × (−3) = −90 J.

questions.q: An ideal machine, in which no energy is wasted, would have an efficiency of:
questions.x: If no energy is wasted, all the input becomes useful output, so efficiency = 100%. Real machines always fall short of this.

questions.q: A cyclist rides 314 m along a circular track of radius 50 m. Taking π = 3.14, his angular displacement about the centre is:
o: 0.16 rad, a small fraction of a revolution
questions.x: θ = s/r = 314/50 = 6.28 rad = 2π rad, which is exactly one revolution. Dividing the radius by the arc gives the wrong 0.16.

questions.q: A fluid flow in which the velocity at a fixed point keeps changing with time is called:
questions.x: In steady flow the velocity at each point is constant in time; if it changes, the flow is unsteady. Incompressibility and viscosity are separate properties.

questions.q: A tiny dust particle settles slowly through still air, while a stone is thrown fast through the same air. The flow of air around them is:
o: Turbulent around the dust particle and laminar around the stone
Laminar around the dust particle and turbulent around the stone
questions.x: Very small, slow objects keep the flow laminar (Stokes' law works for them). A fast-moving stone exceeds the critical speed and leaves a turbulent wake, as most practical flows do.

questions.q: A garden hose of internal cross-sectional area 3 cm² carries water at 1 m s⁻¹. The nozzle at its end has an area of 0.5 cm². The speed of the water leaving the nozzle is:
questions.x: v₂ = A₁v₁/A₂ = 3 × 1 / 0.5 = 6 m s⁻¹. This is why narrowing the outlet makes the jet go further.

questions.q: A spinning ball curves sideways as it travels through the air. The textbook explanation is that:
o: The ball's weight acts sideways while it spins
The air density is greater on one side of the ball
The air moves faster on one side of the ball than the other, creating a pressure difference across it
The ball gains mass while it spins
questions.x: Spin makes the air flow faster past one side, so the pressure there is lower; the pressure difference pushes the ball sideways.

questions.q: Which of the following can carry both transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves?
questions.x: Solids resist both compression and sideways shear, so they carry both kinds of wave. Gases and liquids in bulk carry only longitudinal waves.

questions.q: Two coherent sources vibrate in phase and send waves of equal amplitude A to a point P with a path difference of 2λ. The amplitude at P is:
questions.x: A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths gives constructive interference, so the amplitudes add to 2A. The intensity, not the amplitude, becomes 4 times that of one wave.

questions.q: In a progressive transverse wave on a string, the particles that have the greatest kinetic energy at a given instant are those:
o: Halfway between the mean position and a crest
questions.x: A vibrating particle moves fastest as it passes through its mean position, so its kinetic energy is greatest there. At crests and troughs it is momentarily at rest.

questions.q: Laplace assumed that the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave in air obey:
questions.x: Laplace treated the changes as adiabatic, for which PVᵞ = constant. PV = constant is Boyle's law, the isothermal assumption made by Newton.

questions.q: An organ pipe of length 0.85 m has one end closed. Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹. Ignoring end correction, what is the lowest frequency above the fundamental that it can sound?
questions.x: Fundamental f₁ = v/4L = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz. A closed pipe gives only odd harmonics, so the next one is 3 × 100 = 300 Hz, not 200 Hz.

questions.q: Two identical sound waves of equal amplitude meet at a point exactly out of phase. A listener at that point hears:
o: A sound of double the frequency
questions.x: Equal waves in opposite phase cancel (destructive interference), so the point is quiet. The energy is redistributed to the loud points, not destroyed.

questions.q: Water falls 84 m down a waterfall. If all its potential energy became internal energy of the water, its temperature rise would be about (g = 10 m s⁻², specific heat of water 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹):
questions.x: For each kilogram, mgh = mcΔT, so ΔT = gh/c = 10 × 84 ÷ 4200 = 840 ÷ 4200 = 0.2 K. The mass cancels.

questions.q: If an ideal gas has Cv equal to twice the gas constant, what is the value of γ = Cp/Cv?
questions.x: Cp = Cv + R = 3R, so γ = 3R ÷ 2R = 1.5. Giving Cp/Cv as Cv/Cp gives 0.67.

questions.q: Two +1 nC charges sit 2 m from each other. Find the field at a spot on the same line, outside the pair, 1 m from the nearer charge. (k = 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
o: 8 N C⁻¹, directed away from the pair
9 N C⁻¹, directed towards the pair
10 N C⁻¹, directed away from the pair
questions.x: From the nearer charge (1 m): 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹ / 1² = 9 N C⁻¹. From the farther one (3 m): 9/9 = 1 N C⁻¹. Both point away from the positive charges, i.e. in the same direction there, so the total is 10 N C⁻¹.

questions.q: Moving away from an isolated charge, the value of V is inversely proportional to:
questions.x: V = kq/r, so V is inversely proportional to r itself. Inverse proportion to r² belongs to the electric field.

questions.q: A particle of mass 2 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge 4 × 10⁻⁶ C is placed in a uniform electric field of 500 N C⁻¹. Ignoring gravity, its acceleration is:
The resistance of a wire is 5 Ω at 0 °C and 6 Ω at 100 °C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of its material is:
questions.x: α = (R − R₀) ÷ (R₀ t) = (6 − 5) ÷ (5 × 100) = 1/500 = 2 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹. Dividing by 6 instead of 5 gives about 1.7 × 10⁻³.

questions.q: When the load resistance R is made much larger than the internal resistance r of a source, the efficiency of power transfer:
o: Approaches 100%, though the power delivered becomes small
Is the same as at maximum power transfer
questions.x: Efficiency = R/(R + r), which approaches 1 when R ≫ r. But the current, and so the power, falls as R becomes very large.

questions.q: The vector area of a flat surface is a vector whose magnitude is the area and whose direction is:
o: Along the surface, parallel to one edge
Along the normal to the surface
Along the tangent at the edge
questions.x: Vector area points along the normal (perpendicular) to the plane of the surface. Its magnitude is the area.

questions.q: A magnetic flux density of 0.02 T, expressed in gauss, is:
For a single loop, the induced emf at any instant equals the magnitude of the slope of the graph of:
questions.x: ε = −dΦ/dt, which is the gradient of the flux–time graph. A flat part of that graph means zero emf.

questions.q: Which radiation from the Sun causes sunburn and is also used to sterilise surfaces in hospitals?
questions.x: Ultraviolet radiation damages skin cells (sunburn) and kills bacteria, so UV lamps are used for sterilisation.

questions.q: When a PN junction is connected in forward bias, the holes in the p-region and the free electrons in the n-region are pushed:
questions.x: The positive terminal repels holes and the negative terminal repels electrons, driving both towards the junction, where they cross and recombine.

questions.q: The energy carried by a single photon is directly proportional to the light's:
questions.x: E = hf, so photon energy rises in direct proportion to frequency. It is inversely proportional to wavelength and does not depend on amplitude.

questions.q: A photon of energy 15 eV is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state (−13.6 eV). What happens?
o: The electron rises to the n = 2 level
The photon cannot be absorbed because 15 eV matches no level difference
The atom is ionised and the electron leaves with 1.4 eV of kinetic energy
The electron rises to n = 3 and keeps 1.4 eV
questions.x: 15 eV is more than the 13.6 eV ionisation energy, so the electron is freed; the extra 15 − 13.6 = 1.4 eV becomes its kinetic energy. Above ionisation, any photon energy can be absorbed.

questions.q: The nuclei ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N have the same:
questions.x: Both have A = 14. Carbon has 6 protons and 8 neutrons while nitrogen has 7 of each, so Z and N differ.

questions.q: "The rough bark scraped her palms, and the icy stream numbed her bare feet." The imagery in this line mainly appeals to the sense of:
questions.x: Rough bark scraping the palms and icy water numbing the feet are both felt through the skin, so the imagery appeals to touch.

questions.q: Report in indirect speech: Ali said, "Alas! I have failed."
o: Ali exclaimed with sorrow that he has failed.
Ali said alas that he had failed.
Ali exclaimed with sorrow that he had failed.
Ali asked with sorrow whether he had failed.
questions.x: An exclamation of grief is reported with 'exclaimed with sorrow', the interjection is dropped, and 'have failed' becomes 'had failed'.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "The team lost its best player in the first half; ___, it went on to win the match."
questions.x: Winning after losing the best player is unexpected, so a contrast word, 'nevertheless', fits; 'consequently' and 'therefore' show result.

questions.q: "The referee remained impartial throughout the final, applying the rules equally to both teams." The word 'impartial' means:
questions.x: 'Impartial' means not favouring either side; the clue is that he applied the rules equally to both teams.

questions.q: In a drama, the audience knows that the sweets have been poisoned, but the hero happily offers them to his guests. This is an example of:
questions.x: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not; verbal irony is saying the opposite of what one means.

questions.q: Change into the passive voice: "Do not touch the wires."
o: Let the wires not be touched.
questions.x: A negative command becomes passive with 'Let' + object + 'not be' + past participle.

questions.q: Find the error: "Every morning my father is reading the newspaper before breakfast."
questions.x: A daily habit takes the simple present, so it should be 'reads', not the present continuous 'is reading'.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "By studying every night is how she passed the exam."
o: By studying every night was how she passed the exam.
By studying every night, is how she passed the exam.
She passed the exam by studying every night.
Studying every night is how by she passed the exam.
questions.x: A phrase beginning with 'By' cannot be the subject of 'is'; this mixes two structures. 'She passed the exam by studying every night' has a clear subject and verb.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "The new hostel has many furnitures in every room."
o: The new hostel has many furniture in every room.
The new hostel has a lot of furnitures in every room.
The new hostel has much furnitures in every room.
The new hostel has a lot of furniture in every room.
questions.x: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun: it has no plural form and takes 'much' or 'a lot of', not 'many'.

questions.q: Statement: Should the medical entry test be held twice a year? Argument I: Yes, a student who is ill on the test day would get another chance within the same year. Argument II: No, students would get bored of preparing for the same test. Which argument is strong?
o: Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
questions.x: Argument I gives a real, important benefit directly linked to the proposal. Argument II rests on a trivial, personal feeling rather than a serious consequence, so it is weak.

questions.q: Which pair of numbers shows that the claim "The sum of any two prime numbers is even" is false?
questions.x: 2 + 3 = 5, which is odd, so this one pair disproves the claim. The other pairs are both odd primes, and their sums are even.

questions.q: Find the next number: 1, 2, 2, 4, 8, 32, ?
questions.x: From the third term on, each term is the product of the two before it: 2x2=4, 2x4=8, 4x8=32, so next is 8 x 32 = 256.

questions.q: Find the next number: 4, 11, 18, 25, ?
questions.x: Each term is 7 more than the one before: 25 + 7 = 32.

questions.q: In a class of 35 students ranked by marks with no ties, Ayesha is 10th from the top. Sana is five places below Ayesha. What is Sana's rank from the bottom?
questions.x: Sana is 15th from the top. Rank from the bottom = 35 - 15 + 1 = 21st.

questions.q: Five boxes, blue, green, red, white and yellow, are stacked one on top of another. The green box is at the bottom, and the yellow box is directly on top of it. The blue box is directly on top of the red box. The white box is somewhere above the blue box. Which box is in the middle of the stack?
questions.x: Green is 1st and yellow 2nd from the bottom. Red, blue and white fill places 3 to 5, with blue on red and white above blue, so red is 3rd: the middle.

questions.q: Statement: Several schoolchildren in Faisalabad were bitten by stray dogs near their school. Courses of action: I. The city authorities should take steps to control stray dogs near the school. II. The bitten children should be given the anti-rabies vaccine as advised by doctors. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Action I prevents further bites, and action II protects the children already bitten. Each deals with a real part of the problem.

questions.q: Rashid claims that a full moon makes people behave more aggressively, because the emergency ward was very busy on the last full-moon night. What is the best way to test his claim?
o: Ask Rashid how strongly he believes it
Compare emergency records over many full-moon nights with many other nights
Check whether the moon was bright on that one night
Count how many people looked at the moon that night
questions.x: One busy night proves nothing. Comparing many full-moon nights with many ordinary nights would show whether any real difference exists.

questions.q: After an operation, Fatima feels she will never walk normally again. Her doctor says most patients with her operation walk normally again after regular physiotherapy. Which conclusion is both logical and positive?
o: She will certainly never walk again
By doing regular physiotherapy as advised, she has a good chance of walking normally again
She will walk normally even without physiotherapy
Physiotherapy is useful only for athletes
questions.x: The doctor's information shows that most such patients recover with physiotherapy. Her chance is good if she follows the advice, so hopeless fear is not justified.
